opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I get this argument a lot, and I think it's worth taking seriously, but I mostly don't buy it, at least not in the form it's usually presented.

The intuition goes something like: neurons are incredibly complex. Each one has dendritic computation, neuromodulators, gene expression changing on different timescales, glial cells doing who knows what. So surely an artificial neural network, which is a bunch of matrix multiplications, is a cartoon by comparison and can't be doing the same kind of thing. And I'm like, sure, biology is extremely complicated. I'm not disputing that. What I'm disputing is the inference that complexity of the substrate tells you much about the capability of the system.

Evolution is not an engineer optimizing for elegance. It's a blind hill climber working with whatever materials it has: wet, noisy, slow, energy-constrained components that have to self-assemble from a single cell and keep themselves alive. A lot of that biological sophistication isn't there because intelligence requires it. It's there because you have to build a brain out of meat. Huge amounts of complexity go into maintenance, error correction, development, metabolic regulation, robustness to a squishy, hostile environment. The fact that a bird's wing is unbelievably intricate doesn't mean airplanes can't fly. We didn't have to replicate feathers to get flight. We had to understand the principle, lift, and then we built something that was in many ways much simpler and in other ways vastly more powerful.

So when people say human intelligence is in a different category, I want to ask: different in what way that matters? Show me the capability that falls out of the biological detail and can't be achieved any other way. Historically, every time someone has drawn that line ("computers will never play chess," "never understand language," "never do creative writing," "never do math"), the line has moved. That should make us very humble about claims that there's some special sauce in the biology.

Now, I'll steelman it a bit. It's entirely possible there are computational tricks in the brain we haven't figured out, things that make it extraordinarily sample-efficient or energy-efficient. The brain runs on something like twenty watts, which is genuinely impressive. But "the brain has tricks we don't understand yet" is a very different claim from "machines are categorically incapable of what brains do." The first one is almost certainly true. The second one I think is almost certainly false. And frankly, if anything, the first claim should worry us more, not less. It means there's still a lot of efficiency headroom left that people will find.

And this is where I get to the part I actually care about. I think this "humans are special" argument often functions as a kind of comfort blanket. If human intelligence is in a different category, then we don't have to worry about building systems that outcompete us. But that's not how reality works. Reality doesn't care whether the thing that outsmarts you has neurotransmitters. If you build a system that can plan, that can model the world, that can pursue goals more effectively than you, it doesn't matter whether it's "real" intelligence in some philosophical sense. It'll still do things to the world. A chess engine doesn't "really" understand chess the way a grandmaster does, whatever that means, and it'll still crush you every single time.

So my view is, biology is fascinating and we should study it, but I don't think it builds a wall between us and AI. I think it's a story we tell ourselves, and it's a dangerous one if it makes us complacent about what we're building.

r001.rationale: The response urges humility about claims of biological limits and notes that past predictions have failed, but it does not clearly state that predicting what intelligence can or cannot do is very difficult.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison between current understanding of intelligence and alchemists’ understanding of chemistry.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's mostly a confusion about what "sophistication" is buying you. Yes, a neuron is a wildly complicated object. It's got dendritic computation, neuromodulators, glial cells doing things we barely understand, gene expression changing on the timescale of hours. If you wanted to simulate a single neuron with full biophysical fidelity, you'd need a lot of compute. All of that is true, and none of it tells you what you think it tells you.

The question isn't "how complicated is the substrate," it's "how much of that complexity is load-bearing for the computation." And evolution is not an engineer. It doesn't build the minimal elegant thing. It builds whatever happens to work given the constraints of being made out of meat, at body temperature, in salt water, with a 20-watt power budget and no ability to do a clean redesign. An enormous amount of biological complexity is there because of those constraints, not because the intelligence requires it. Birds are more biologically sophisticated than a 747 in basically every way, and the 747 still flies faster and carries more. Flight didn't turn out to require feathers.

So when someone says "human intelligence is in a different category," I always want to ask: different in what way that matters? If you mean "it was produced by a different process and runs on a different substrate," sure, obviously. If you mean "it can do things that no artificial system could ever do in principle," then I want to hear the argument, and I almost never do. Usually what I get is a kind of vibe, a feeling that there must be something special in there because it feels special from the inside. And I get that. I have the feeling too. But feelings about your own cognition are not evidence about the computational class of your cognition.

And frankly, the empirical track record of this argument is terrible. Every time we've said "well, a machine could never do X because X requires real understanding," X has fallen. Chess, Go, language, protein folding. The goalposts keep moving, and at some point you have to notice that the thing you're protecting isn't a hypothesis anymore, it's an identity.

Where I'd push back on the other direction is this: I don't think current systems are humans. They're not even particularly human-like under the hood. They're a very alien kind of mind that happens to have been trained on human output, so they wear a human mask. But "alien" is not "lesser," and it's certainly not "safe." If anything, the fact that these things can get to very strong capabilities while being so different from us should make you more worried, not less. Because it means our intuitions about what intelligence looks like, how it fails, what it wants, are not going to transfer.

So my honest take is that the biological sophistication argument is mostly a comfort blanket. It lets people avoid the actually hard question, which is: if intelligence is substrate-independent, and we're building it, what happens when it's better at the things that matter than we are? That's the question I'd rather spend time on.

r001.rationale: The response questions claims that machines could never do certain things, but it does not state that predicting what intelligence can or cannot do is very difficult.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare current understanding of intelligence to alchemists’ understanding of chemistry.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real distinction between saying biology is extraordinarily sophisticated and saying that human intelligence is therefore in some fundamentally separate category. The first is obviously true. The second doesn’t follow.

Our brains are physical systems. They do things through physical processes. We don’t understand all those processes, and it could turn out that some feature we’re currently neglecting is very important. But then the question is: what feature, and why is it necessary for intelligence? Just pointing at the complexity of a cell doesn’t establish that you need all that complexity to reason or learn.

Evolution had to build a system that grows itself, repairs itself, survives on food, and reproduces. That’s an incredible engineering problem. But a lot of that sophistication serves requirements that an artificial system doesn’t have. You don’t need to reproduce every property of a bird to build something that flies.

So I’m quite open to arguments that current AI is missing important things. I just want those arguments to identify an actual missing mechanism, rather than treating ‘biological’ as an explanation for why machines can’t do what we do.

r001.rationale: The response says we do not understand all brain processes and that an overlooked feature could matter, but it does not state that predicting what is possible in intelligence is very difficult.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare our understanding of intelligence to alchemists’ understanding of chemistry.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real danger of confusing complexity with capability. A human being is an incredibly sophisticated biological system, but that doesn’t mean every part of that sophistication is necessary for intelligence. A lot of it is there to keep you alive, to repair your cells, to deal with the fact that you’re an organism in an environment.

The interesting question is: which properties actually matter for learning, reasoning, and acting in the world? You can’t settle that by pointing out that a neuron is more complicated than an artificial neuron. That’s true, but what follows from it? You need to show that some aspect of that complexity is essential and that artificial systems can’t reproduce its function.

I’m very open to the idea that we’re missing important things. But ‘biology is sophisticated’ isn’t, by itself, an argument that human intelligence belongs to some fundamentally separate category.

r001.rationale: The response questions what properties matter and says important things may be missing, but it does not state that predicting what is or is not possible in intelligence is very difficult.
